cards.text: Paul has been teaching in Corinth, and he stays on there for quite some time. Now it's time to say goodbye to the brothers. And on his way out, in Cenchrea, he gets his head shaved. No warning. Just straight to the barber.

cards.question: Why does Paul get his head shaved in Cenchrea?

answers.text: To keep a vow he had made
To mark his last day in Corinth
To get ready for the long voyage

cards.question: Paul sets sail for Syria, and he's got company. ___ and ___ are on the boat with him.

cards.text: Priscilla and Aquila are a married couple, tentmakers just like Paul, and he worked with them in Corinth (Acts 18:2-3). When the ship reaches Ephesus, Paul leaves them there and heads into the synagogue on his own.

cards.question: Inside the synagogue in Ephesus, what does Paul do?

cards.text: The Jews in Ephesus ask Paul to stay a while longer. Friend, when nobody in the room is checking the time, you've got their attention.

cards.question: Paul agrees to stay a while longer in Ephesus.

cards.text: But Paul doesn't leave them with nothing. On his way out, he makes them a promise, and it comes with one condition.

cards.question: What's the condition on Paul's promise to come back to Ephesus?

answers.text: If the synagogue writes to him
If the winds turn his way

cards.text: "I will come back to you if God is willing." Most honest travel plan I ever heard. ME? I said I'd be right back on that counter, and then came the junk drawer.
Then Paul sails from Ephesus and lands at Caesarea. From there, he goes up to greet the church.

cards.question: From Caesarea, Paul goes up and greets the church at ___.

cards.text: Then he goes down to Antioch and spends some time there. After that, he's back on the road, place to place through Galatia and Phrygia. This man's mileage is UNREAL.

cards.question: As Paul travels through Galatia and Phrygia, what does he do for all the disciples?

cards.text: Meanwhile, back in Ephesus, there's a new face in town. Apollos, a Jew from Alexandria.

cards.question: Apollos is an eloquent man, well versed in the Scriptures.

cards.text: He's been taught the way of the Lord, he's fervent in spirit, and he teaches about Jesus accurately. This man can PREACH. But there's one gap in what he knows.

cards.question: Apollos teaches accurately about Jesus, though he knows only the baptism of ___.

cards.text: Apollos starts speaking boldly in the synagogue. And guess who's in the crowd? Priscilla and Aquila.

cards.question: After hearing Apollos, what do Priscilla and Aquila do?

answers.text: Take him aside and explain the way of God more accurately
Correct him right there in front of the whole synagogue
Tell him to stop teaching until Paul comes back

cards.text: No calling him out in front of everybody. They pull him aside and fill in what he's missing. Friend, that's how you fix a blurry stamp. GENTLY.

cards.question: When Apollos decides to cross over to Achaia, the brothers try to talk him out of it.

cards.text: They encourage him and write to the disciples in Achaia to welcome him. A letter of recommendation! The only paperwork I ever came with was a price sticker that said 25 cents.

cards.question: In Achaia, Apollos is a great help to the believers. How does he prove in public debate that Jesus is the Christ?

findings.problem: The opening card has 4 sentences: 'Paul has been teaching…', 'Now it's time…', 'And on his way out…', 'No warning.' plus 'Just straight to the barber.' That goes over the limit for an opening card.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on.

findings.problem: 'Paul has been teaching in Corinth' is a fact from the earlier passage (Acts 18:11). It carries no reference.

rule.text: References. Every Bible fact he states carries its reference.

findings.problem: Priscilla and Aquila first show up as the answers to this card, before anyone has said who they are. Card 4 introduces them only after the baker has had to pick their names. The baker has nothing to reason from.

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: The two blanks hold names that can swap places. 'Aquila and Priscilla' is just as true to Acts 18:18 as 'Priscilla and Aquila', but the blank fields mark only one order as right.
findings.question: When a two-blank card's right answers could reasonably fill either blank, should the code accept either order, or should the card be rewritten so only one order makes sense?

findings.problem: The joke 'I said I'd be right back on that counter, and then came the junk drawer' invents a new moment in his backstory. In the backstory he was picked up and slid into the drawer, and he never promised to come back.

rule.text: His own world isn't Bible fact. His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them. His jokes can make up small moments and habits around his bakery.

findings.problem: This card only repeats the answer to card 9 (the 'if God is willing' quote) and reacts to it. It doesn't move the passage forward. Acts 18:21's sailing is told on card 11.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage. No recap cards.

findings.problem: This card restates the answer to card 6 (they took him aside and filled in what he was missing). It adds no new part of the passage.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage. No recap cards.

findings.problem: In 'that's how you fix a blurry stamp. GENTLY.', the comparison doesn't share the core action, which is correcting someone privately. A blurry stamp isn't fixed by pulling it aside, and his own stamp was made new by God, not fixed gently. The line also calls Apollos 'blurry' when Acts 18:25 says he taught accurately. 'GENTLY' adds a manner the text doesn't state.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action. … It clicks instantly for any adult, with no explaining. If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.
